title: The Nonclustered Index Tipping Point
description: Past the tipping point a non-covering index costs more than a scan, so the optimizer scans; a covering index brings back the seek. Why it matters: understanding the tipping point is essential for correctly diagnosing why the optimizer "suddenly" stops using an index that used to work fine.
narrative:
## What This Lesson Is About

Imagine you need to find every red car in a giant parking garage. If you're looking for just two or three red cars out of thousands, it's worth walking straight to the specific spots you know have red cars, ignoring everything else. But if half the cars in the garage are red, it's actually faster to just walk every row of the garage once, glancing at each car as you pass, than to keep consulting a list of "here's where each red car is" and constantly detouring back and forth between rows to reach every single one. This lesson is about that exact trade-off inside SQL Server's query optimizer, and about why having an index doesn't automatically mean the optimizer will use it.

**What this lesson's topic actually is.** A nonclustered index is a separate, compact structure built on one or more columns that lets SQL Server jump directly to matching rows instead of reading the whole table — like the "list of where each red car is parked" in the analogy above. But a nonclustered index typically doesn't contain every column of the table; if your query needs columns the index doesn't have, SQL Server has to take an extra step, called a "key lookup," to go back to the main table and fetch the rest of the row's data for every single match the index found. This lesson is about what happens when the number of matches gets large: at some point, doing one key lookup per matching row becomes more expensive, in total, than simply reading the entire table once — and when that happens, the optimizer, quite reasonably, refuses to use the index at all, even though it exists and is a perfectly valid, correct choice for satisfying the filter.

**Why this happens in real databases.** It's tempting to think "I have an index on this column, so any query filtering on that column will be fast." That's true only up to a point. An index that doesn't include every column a query needs (a "non-covering" index) is only cheap when relatively few rows match, because each match costs one extra trip back to the main table. As the fraction of the table that matches your filter grows, those extra trips add up, and eventually a single sequential read of the entire table — no jumping around, no extra trips, just one pass — becomes cheaper overall, even though it touches every row instead of just the matching ones.

**How it happens mechanically inside SQL Server.** The optimizer doesn't decide "use the index" or "scan the table" based on gut feeling — it estimates an actual cost, in an internal unit roughly proportional to disk I/O and CPU work, for each candidate plan, and picks whichever estimate is lower. For the index-seek-plus-lookup plan, that cost is roughly: the cost of seeking into the index once, plus the cost of one key lookup for every single row that matches. Each key lookup is a small, random access back into the main table's storage — cheap individually, but the costs are all added together, one per matching row. For the full-scan plan, the cost is roughly fixed: read every page of the table sequentially, once, regardless of how many rows match the filter. As the number of matching rows grows, the seek-plus-lookup plan's total cost climbs roughly in proportion (more matches, more individual lookups), while the scan's cost stays essentially flat (it was always going to read the whole table regardless). At some crossover point — sometimes called the "tipping point" — the accumulated cost of all those individual lookups overtakes the flat cost of just scanning everything, and past that point, the optimizer's cost-based logic correctly favors the scan, even though the index technically "could" answer the query.

**Why this matters in production.** Understanding the tipping point is essential for correctly diagnosing a common, confusing complaint: "I created an index on this exact column, and SQL Server just isn't using it — is the optimizer broken?" It isn't broken; it's making a legitimate, cost-based decision that a non-covering index simply isn't worth using once a large enough share of the table matches the filter. This trips people up because it feels like having *any* index on the filtered column should help, when in reality, a non-covering index's usefulness genuinely depends on what fraction of the table a given query actually touches — there's no single universal percentage where this always happens (it depends on row width, page layout, and I/O costs), but the underlying shape of the trade-off always holds: fewer matches favor the seek, more matches favor the scan. The fix in this lesson isn't to force the index (which would just make things artificially worse, generating exactly the flood of expensive individual lookups the optimizer was correctly trying to avoid) — it's to make the index "covering," meaning it includes every column the query needs directly inside the index itself, via an `INCLUDE` clause. A covering index needs zero key lookups no matter how many rows match, because everything the query needs is already sitting right there in the index — which pushes the tipping point far out, or removes the trade-off from the equation entirely, letting an index seek beat a full scan even for tens of thousands of matching rows.

**Try it yourself.** The scenario below runs a filter matching a large share of the table and shows you the Clustered Index Scan the optimizer chose despite a nonclustered index existing on the filtered column. Try forcing the index with a hint and compare the logical reads — you'll see the forced plan actually costs *more* in reads than the scan the optimizer picked on its own, confirming its decision was correct given the non-covering index. Then add the `INCLUDE`d columns to make the index covering, remove the hint, and re-run: now the optimizer chooses the seek on its own, because the lookup cost that used to make the scan cheaper no longer exists at all.

## Scenario
`SELECT CustomerId, OrderDate, Total, Status FROM Orders WHERE CustomerId <= 800` returns roughly 32,000 rows. There is a nonclustered index on `CustomerId`, yet the plan **ignores it** and scans the whole clustered index.

## Why the optimizer refuses the index
The index `IX_Orders_CustomerId` is **non-covering**: it holds `CustomerId` (and the clustered key `OrderId`) but not `OrderDate`, `Total`, or `Status`. To return those columns via the index the engine would seek, then perform a **key lookup** into the clustered index for *every* matching row. At ~32k rows those random lookups cost far more than simply scanning the table once, so the optimizer picks a **Clustered Index Scan**.

This is the **tipping point**: once a predicate matches enough of the table that the cost of a key lookup per row outweighs a single sequential scan, a non-covering nonclustered index stops being worthwhile and a full scan wins. There's no fixed universal percentage — the exact threshold shifts with row width and I/O pattern and is often cited anywhere from the low single digits to a few tens of percent — but the shape of the tradeoff always holds: below the threshold, seek + lookups win; above it, the scan does. This query's 16% (32,000 of 200,000 rows) sits comfortably past it.

## What to look for
- The seed index exists but the plan shows a **Clustered Index Scan** on `Orders`, not a seek.
- Forcing the seek (with a hint) would expose thousands of extra reads from key lookups.

## The fix
Raise the index **past** the tipping point by making it **covering**: add the needed columns with `INCLUDE`. A covering index needs no lookups, so a range **Index Seek** reads only the qualifying leaf pages and beats the scan even for tens of thousands of rows.

_This query returns thousands of rows, so we grade on the plan operator and per-table logical reads, not the row set._
startingQuery: SELECT CustomerId, OrderDate, Total, Status FROM Orders WHERE CustomerId <= 800;
hints: The nonclustered index exists, but the plan is a Clustered Index Scan — the optimizer chose it on purpose.
The index doesn't cover OrderDate/Total/Status, so using it would mean ~32,000 key lookups. Past a certain fraction of the table (the exact threshold varies), a scan is cheaper.
Push the index past the tipping point by covering the query: CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_Orders_Cust_Cov ON Orders(CustomerId) INCLUDE(OrderDate, Total, Status);
